title: Indian American Scholar Roopika Risam Makes Obama's 2026 Summer Reading List
excerpt: Dartmouth professor's book 'Data Empire,' an 11,000-year history of how information shaped power, joins works by Colson Whitehead and Ann Patchett on Obama's annual picks.
body:
• Dartmouth professor Roopika Risam's book 'Data Empire' has been named to Barack Obama's 2026 summer reading list, released July 30.
  • The book traces 11,000 years of how data — from Mesopotamian clay tablets to modern algorithms — has served as a tool of power and control.
  • Risam is a Professor of Digital Humanities and Social Engagement at Dartmouth, with over $4.3 million in research grants from the NEH and Mellon Foundation.
  • 'Data Empire' was previously selected as an NPR and New Scientist summer reading pick.

Dartmouth professor Roopika Risam landed on one of the most influential book recommendation lists in the country this week when Barack Obama included her book Data Empire in his 2026 summer reading picks, released on July 30.

The list, an annual tradition that regularly sends titles surging up bestseller charts, featured 11 books this year. Risam's work sat alongside novels by Colson Whitehead, Ann Patchett, George Saunders, and Tayari Jones — established literary heavyweights who have appeared on Obama's lists before. Risam was the only nonfiction debut author on this year's slate.

What 'Data Empire' Argues

Data Empire: How Information Shaped Human History, published by HarperCollins in the US and Torva/Penguin in the UK, is a sweeping account of how the collection and classification of information has underpinned every form of organized power in human history.

The book begins in Mesopotamia, where rulers pressed marks into clay to track land, people, and grain — establishing a pattern that Risam traces through Han Dynasty records, the Domesday Book, colonial censuses and maps, and into the modern era of algorithmic surveillance and corporate data brokers.

"What has it meant — and what will it mean — when records that once served only to help us remember, come to rule?"

— Roopika Risam, Data Empire

NPR's review called it essential reading for anyone trying to understand the power dynamics of the data economy, noting: "You're probably better served trying to answer with the help of Risam than, say, Alexa or Claude." The book received a starred review from Publishers Weekly and was named a 2026 summer reading pick by both NPR and New Scientist.

The Scholar Behind the Book

Risam is Professor of Film and Media Studies and Digital Humanities and Social Engagement at Dartmouth College, where she also chairs the Film and Media Studies department and directs Graduate Studies in Comparative Literature. Her research sits at the intersection of race, empire, and technology — examining how historical power structures have been encoded into modern digital systems.

Her previous book, New Digital Worlds: Postcolonial Digital Humanities in Theory, Praxis, and Pedagogy, published by Northwestern University Press in 2019, has been taught in more than 150 university courses worldwide. Her work has been supported by over $4.3 million in grants from the National Endowment for the Humanities, the Mellon Foundation, and other funders.

Risam is also known for public-facing digital projects, including Torn Apart/Separados, which visualized the U.S. government's family separation policy at the border during the first Trump administration. She is a past president of the Association for Computers and the Humanities.

Obama's Full 2026 Reading List

The 11-book list blended literary fiction with nonfiction, featuring Kin by Tayari Jones, Cool Machine by Colson Whitehead, Whistler by Ann Patchett, Vigil by George Saunders, A World Appears by Michael Pollan, This Land is Your Land by Beverly Gage, and others. Obama also released his annual summer playlist the same day.

For Indian American academics, Risam's inclusion marks a growing recognition of South Asian scholarship in mainstream American intellectual culture — a space where diaspora voices have increasingly shaped conversations about technology, power, and global history.
